body.p: The Vへん verb ending may be the single most distinctive and recognizable piece of grammar in Kansai-ben. It is the plain non-past negative verb conjugation, analogous to Vない in standard Japanese. In addition, there is also a shortened form: Vん. Thus, standard Japanese's 行かない could be rendered as 行かへん or 行かん in Kansai-ben.
There are a variety of verb negations within the umbrella of Kansai-ben that use these two basic verb negations as a base, with variations depending on region or speaker preference.
Use へん or ん instead of ない.

There are many of different negative forms of 来る depending on many factors, such as region and age. Young people may use こおへん, which is a "neo-dialect", a hybrid of standard Japanese and Kansai-ben.

Using the different transformations described, a standard Japanese verb can end up having a fair number Kansai-ben analogs. For example, the standard Japanese 起きない can variously become: 起きへん, 起きひん, 起けへん, and 起きん.

body.h: The negative form of いる

body.p: Although there is no progressive form (teiru) of いる in standard Japanese, there is a such a form in Kansai-ben--see the いてる for more detail. The negative of this form, which would be the fantastic いてる in standard Japanese, is いてへん.

The standard Japanese negative form of ある is ない; あらない is considered to be an inappropriate in standard Japanese--consider how most people respond to the use of "ain't" in American English in spite of its wide use. However things are different in Kansai-ben, where あらへん and あれへん happily exist as negative forms of ある, heedless to prescriptions of standard Japanese.
The negative progressive form Vている is quite varied. Besides Vてへん, for example, there are Vてない (standard/neo-dialect), Vとらん (Kobe), and Vとらへん (Osaka).

body.p: Looking from standard Japanese to Kansai-ben, there are some differences in the final vowels of the te-form and ta-form when the verb ends with [au], [ou], or [uu] sounds.
The first case is for verbs where the dictionary form is just two characters (かう, すう, etc.). In this case the sound before the う extends (vowel extension).
The second case is for the other verbs. In this case the sound before the う can extend (vowel extension), but not necessarily.
Like standard Japanese, particles are tend to be omitted, especially in casual speech. However, there are some differences in the ways that they are dropped in Kansai-ben and standard Japanese.

In most Japanese textbooks, the destination particle (i.e., 学校に行く) can be either に or へ. However, in Kansai, most people just use へ. body.p: The Kansai-ben final particles で and ど have a function that draws attention to something that the listener might not know. In addition, they can also be used for assertion, question, admonition, and occasionally warning. These final particles are like よ and ぜ in standard Japanese.

body.p: The further addition of a な, giving かいな can add an additional feeling of surprise, confusion, anger, or others. See the かいな page for more details.
In Kansai-ben, ねん, てん, ん, のん, and たん are used in queries, asking for reasons, and giving explanations.

The standard sentence endings のだ and んだ may become ねん and てん in Kansai-ben. The main difference between the two is that while ねん is mainly used in the non-past tense, てん is always used in the past tense.

Similarly, the standard sentence ending の may become ん, のん, or たん in Kansai-ben. It should be noted that ん and のん have essentially the same meaning, with the difference decided by region or speaker preference. Again, similar to the above, while ん and のん are used in the non-past tense, たん is only used in the past-tense (the た in たん is considered to be a part in ta-form of the verbs, adjectives, and nouns that comes in front of たん).
It should be highlighted that just like their counterparts in standard Japanese, ねん and てん are used to express a more emphatic feeling than ん, のん, and たん.
It should also be noted that the てん mentioned here is not related to the てる／てん of verb conjugation.

The standard Japanese endings __じゃないか, __ではないか, and __じゃん can become __やん, __やんか/やんけ, and __がな respectively in Kansai-ben.
These Kansai sentence endings can also be used in the same way as __んだよ in standard Japanese.
There are many uses for these sentence endings; common ones are confirmation, excuses, accusation, notification, and persuasion. The function changes depending on the situation and tone. The __がな ending is used more often by older people.

table.caption: ＿＿たんやん
rows: あの人、実は彼女(が)いたんだよ。
あの人、実は彼女おったんやん(か)。

table.caption: ＿＿んやがな
rows: 明日、まごが来るんだよ。
明日、まご来るんやがな。

body.p: やん, やんか, やんけ, and がな can be used with ですor ます for politeness, but are rarely used in a formal setting.

table.caption: ＿＿ましたやんか
rows: 昨日、電話すると言ったじゃないですか。
昨日、電話する言いましたやんか。
Didn't I say that I was going to call you yesterday?

table.caption: politeness level
rows: 昨日、電話すると言ったじゃないですか。
昨日、電話する言いましたやんか。
昨日、電話する言うたやんか。

body.p:
Prefix ど can emphasize the meaning of the word, and it is more common in Kansai.
One should be warned that this prefix has a certain rude/older man feel to it and should only be used if one knows what they're doing.

table.caption: Example with どえらい
rows: 今日はものすごい雨だなあ。仕事行くのいやだなあ。
今日はどえらい雨やなあ。仕事行くんいややなあ。
Geez, it's raining so much today. I don't wanna go to work.

body.p:
In general, ど is used with negative words, not positive words (such as きれい).
However, there are some exceptions. For example, えらい (in the sense of "very") can take ど.

table.caption: どえらい
rows: あの子ものすごくかわいいなあ。
あの子どえらいかえらしなあ。

body.p: ど is often used in abusive language.

table.caption: どたま
rows:
こら、このスケベ野郎！何オレの女をジロジロ見てんだよ！
頭をぶんなぐってやるぞ！

ワレ、このどスケベが。何ワシの女ジロジロ見とんねん！
どたまかち割ったろか！
Hey, you perv! Quit staring at my girl. I'm gunna hafta smack you upside the head.

body.p: The ど-prefixed words which have a neutral meaning, such as ど根性, ど真ん中, and ど迫力, are commonly used even outside of Kansai.

title: Suffix “さん” and “ちゃん”

body.p: In Kansai-ben, the honorific title さん and ちゃん can be used for non-humans, such as for food or greetings. This usage my originate with the polite words and phrases from court language.

table.caption: おかいさん
rows: 今日のお昼ごはん、おかゆでいい？
今日のお昼、おかいさんでええか。
Can we have porridge for lunch?

It doesn't matter how cute she it if her personality is bad.

rows: おいしくなくても食べられたらいいじゃない。

Even if it's not good, you should be happy you can eat at all.

table.caption: na-Adj (affirmative) かて
rows: いくらしずかであったとしても、こんな不便な所はちょっとね。

It doesn't matter how quiet it is, the location isn't really very convenient.

便利やなかったかて、しずかでええとこやな。
Even though it's not convenient, it is really nice and quiet.

rows: アメリカとカナダに*も住んだことあるんだ。
アメリカとカナダにかて住んだことあんねん。

body.p: *Like standard Japanese, かて can be used with other particles such as に, から, で, and と.

table.caption: Nやったかて (degree)
rows: 学生で(あって)も、割引ないんだよ。
学生やったかて、割引*あらへんのや。
Even if you're a student, there is no discount.

body.p: *割引 = discount
Some people use the standard も instead of かて. When older people use も, a euphonic change often occur in i-adjectives.

body.h: そやかて, そうかて, and せやかて

body.p: The standard conjunctions for showing disagreement (それでも and でも) may become そやかて, そうかて, or せやかて.

rows:
いつまで食べているんだ。また太るよ。
え〜、でもおいしいんだもん。やめられないよ。

いつまで食べてんねん。また太るで。
え〜、そやかておいしいねんもん。やめられへんわ。

You're still eating? You're gunna get fat.
But it tastes sooo good. I can't stop.

body.p: The standard Japanese conjunctions for providing a reason, から and ので, may become よって and さかい in Kansai-ben (with the choice depending on the area or personal background such as age).
よって is mostly used by older people while さかい is used by a wider range of ages. In addition, younger people may opt to just use から and ので with a Kansai-ben intonation.
It should also be noted that さかい may become さかいに, さかいで, or さけ, with the difference depending on the region or speaker preference.

rows: 明日、先生のところに行くから、わたしておくよ。
明日、先生とこ行くさかい、わたしとくわ。
I'll be seeing the teacher tomorrow, so I'll give it to them.

body.h: Negative: へんよって, へんさかい

body.p: Like the standard から and ので, negative marker comes before よって and さかい.

table.caption: へんよって
rows: 明日は会社ないからいっぱい寝られるよ。
明日は会社あらへんよってごっつう寝られるわ。
I don't have work tomorrow, so I can sleep in.

body.h: Polite form (long form): でっさかい, まっさかい

body.p: Adding です or ます in front of よって and さかい can make the sentence more polite. In the case of さかい, devoicing may occur before さかい. ですさかい may becomes でっさかい and ますさかい may become まっさかい.

table.caption: まっさかい
rows: ３時ごろ出ますので、４時ごろ着くと思いますよ。
３時ごろ出まっさかい、４時ごろ着くと思いますわ。
I'll be leaving around three, so I think I'll get there around four.

body.p:
The standard conjunctive particle for connecting a reason and a consequence, それで, may become ほんで in Kansai-ben.
In some regions, especially with older people, use ほいで instead.

table.caption: ほんで
rows: 昨日すごくビール飲んだんだ。それで、今日は二日酔いなんだ。
昨日めっちゃビール飲んでん。ほんで、今日は二日酔いやねん。
I had too much beer yesterday. That's why I have a hangover today.

body.p: The standard Vてくれない, when used as a request, may become Vてくれへん and Vてんか in Kansai-ben. Vてんか is a shortened form of Vてくれへん, and may be used more by older people.

rows:
Vてくれへん(か)*
Vてんか

body.p: *The question marker か is often attached.

table.caption: Vてくれへん(か)
rows: これ、持ってくれへん(か)？
Could you hold this for me?

body.p: The standard Vてあげる and Vてやる may become Vたげる and Vたる in Kansai-ben.
The てあ in the standard Japanese Vてあげる can become た in Kansai-ben.
The てや in the standard Japanese Vてやる can become た in Kansai-ben.

table.caption: Vたげる
rows: この本、貸してあげるよ。
You can borrow this book from me.

table.caption: Vたる
rows: 今日、昼ごはんおごってやるよ。
今日、昼めしおごったるわ。

body.p: Vたる is commonly used with somebody you're on good terms with, such as between friends or a parent and a child.

body.h: Request Vたって and report Vたって

body.p: In Kansai-ben, depending on the intonation, Vたって can be used as either a request or to report something. Vたって with a flat intonation is used as a request; with falling intonation it is used as to report something.

table.caption: Vたって
rows: 田中さん、この写真見たって。
Hey Tanaka, would you look at this picture?
田中さん、この写真見たって。
I heard that Tanaka looked at this picture.

body.h: Vたって and requests for the speaker's own sake

body.p: Unlike the analogous for in standard Japanese, in Kansai-ben Vたって can be used in requests for the speaker's own sake.

table.caption: Vたって
rows: もう許してくださいよ。

body.p: Vてもらう in Kansai-ben is the same as standard Japanese, but the past tense from the dictionary form is different. The standard Japanese Vてもらった becomes Vてもろた or Vてもうた in Kansai-ben. もろた is the base for in Kansai-ben, but may become もうた in use.
Please be aware that there is another, completely separate, Vてもうた that expresses repentance and regret.

Vてもうた

table.caption: Vてもろた
rows: これ、彼に買ってもらった服なんだ。
これ、彼に買うてもろた服やねん。
My boyfriend bought these clothes for me.

body.p: The standard Japanese Vてみなさい, when used as an imperative, may become Vてみ in Kansai-ben. Vてみ can be also used to make a suggestion.

rows:
Vてみなさい
Vてみれば？

body.p: *Vowel extension often occurs with the final み.

rows: これ、おいしいよ。食べてみれば？
これ、おいしいで。食べてみぃ。

body.p: Vてみ(ぃ) should not be used with people who are in a superior or respected position.

body.h: Stirring up trouble with Vてみ(ぃ)

body.p: When Vてみ(ぃ) is pronounced with a rising tone, it can be perceived as a challenge, something along the lines of "just try and see".

table.caption: Challenging
rows: なぐれるものならなぐってみろよ。
なぐれるもんならなぐってみぃ。
Do you think you can punch me? (Try and see.)

Vな with a downstep = negative imperative (prohibition)

body.p: Besides Vな, there are other phrases for prohibition such as Vたらあかん and Vんとき. The differences between these three are in the degree of prohibition.

body.p: The standard Japanese expressions for obligation and necessity (see the table below) mostly become Vなあかん in Kansai-ben. However, there are two exceptions that need to be mentioned.
The first exception is Vんとあかん, coming from the standard Japanese Vないといけない. Vなあかん and Vんとあかん have pretty much the same meaning.

The second exception is Vんなららん, coming from the standard Japanese Vなくてはならない. It is an expression that is very similar to Vなあかん, but it is only used for the speaker's own actions. In addition, Vんならん is somewhat softer than Vなあかん and may have a somewhat older feeling.

朝ご飯は毎日食べんとあかんで。

body.p: The prohibition expression Vてはいけない can become Vたらあかん in Kansai-ben. Similarly, the Vないで in standard Japanese can become either Vんといて or Vんとって in Kansai-ben. Paralleling standard Japanese, Vたらあかん expresses strong prohibition while Vんといて and Vんとって express a request for prohibition.
*ら is often omitted.

body.p: The standard Japanese expression to give or ask for permission, Vてもいい, can become Vてもええ in Kansai-ben. Similarly, The standard Japanese Vてもかまわない can become either Vてもかめへん, Vてもかまへん, or Vてもかまん in Kansai-ben. For the differences between the three, please see the usage notes for かめへん, かまへん, and かまん.
*も may be omitted.

body.p: The Vてしまう of standard Japanese, when used to indicate completion, can become Vてまう in Kansai-ben

rows: まだ時間あるから、おさら洗ってしまうよ。
まだ時間あるから、おさら洗ってまうわ。
There's still a little time, I'll finish up the dishes.

body.h: Question forms: Vて(し)まえへん and Vて(し)まわん

body.p:
The question form of Vてまう is Vて(し)まえへん or Vて(し)まわん, with the choice up to the speaker.
Both are pronounced with a rising intonation.

table.caption: Vて(し)まえへん
rows: お父さん帰ってこないうちに食べてしまわない？
お父ちゃん帰ってこんまに食べて(し)まえへん？
Should we finish eating before dad gets home?

body.p: The Vてしまった of standard Japanese, when used as an expression of completion and/or regret, can become Vてしもた or Vても(う)た in Kansai-ben. As the have very much the same feel, the word choice is left to the speaker.

Vてしもた
Vても(う)た

行って しもた
行って も(う)た

rows: あー、おさら割ってしまった。
あー、おさら割ってしもた。

body.h: The function of Vてもうた

body.p: Vてもうた has another function that expresses receiving a favor (see: Vてもろた／Vてもうた). Please compare the different very different meaning and tone of the two:

table.caption: Vてもらった (receiving a favor)
rows: にんじん、きらいだから田中に食べてもらったよ。
にんじん、きらいやから田中に食べてもうたわ。
I don't like carrots so Tanaka ate mine for me.

table.caption: Vてしまった (completion/regret)
rows: もう、おにぎり全部食べてしまったよ。ひとつも残っていないよ。
もう、おにぎり全部食べてもうたで。いっこも残ってないわ。
I already ate all the onigiri. There is nothing left.

body.p: In Kansai-ben, the conditional clause (れ)ば is rarely used. Instead, the conditional clause たら is heavily used--to the extent that it is often used in cases where it would be not consider appropriate in standard Japanese.

rows: 昨日もっと勉強すればよかった。
昨日もっと勉強したらよかった。
I should have studied more yesterday.
電話してくれれば迎えに行くよ。
電話してくれたら迎えに行くで。
If you call me, I'll come and pick you up.

body.p: For most Kansai people, (れ)ば sounds too formal, so たら is used for most any case where one wants to use a conditional expression.

body.h: The negative form of たら

body.p: Since there are various negative forms in Kansai-ben (Vへん／Vん), the negative form of たら clauses are also varied. For example, there are: Vなかったら, Vなんだら, Vんかったら, Vへんかったら, Vへんなんだら, and more...
Although Kansai-ben has the conditional clause __と__ like in standard Japanese, the negative form Vんと can have a different function depending on the intonation.
While Vんと without a downstep is the normal conditional clause, Vんと with a downstep can mean "do not V" or "without doing V", similar to Vないで(ください) and Vせずに in standard Japanese.

rows:
Vないと
Vないで(ください)
Vせずに

table.caption: Vないと (conditional clause)
rows: そろそろ行かないと遅刻するよ。
そろそろ行かんと遅刻するで。
If you don't leave soon you'll be late.

table.caption: Vないで (negative imperative)
rows: 仕事ばっかりしないでたまには私と遊んでよ。
仕事ばっかりせんとたまにはうちと遊んでや。
You shouldn't just work, you know—every once in a while you should come out with me.

table.caption: Vせずに
rows: あいつ、全然仕事せずに携帯ばっかりさわってるよ。
あいつ、いっこも仕事せんと携帯ばっかりいじっとるわ。
He's always fiddling with his cell phone and not doing any work.

body.p: The standard Japanese だ, when used as an assertion, may become や in Kansai-ben. With this, the standard Japanese conditional だったら may become やったら in Kansai-ben, and similarly the conjecture だろう may become やろ(う).
*The final う sound is often devoiced (see dropping "う").

table.caption: ＿＿や (assertion)
rows: 今日もいい天気だなあ。
今日もええ天気やなあ。
It's such a nice day again.

table.caption: ＿＿やったら (conditional)
rows: 明日、いい天気だったら海に行かない？
明日、ええ天気やったら海行けへん？
If the weather's nice tomorrow, do you wanna go to the beach?

table.caption: ＿＿やろ(う) (Conjecture)
rows: 吉田はインフルエンザだから、今日も学校来ないだろう。
吉田はインフルエンザやから、今日も学校けえへんやろ(う)。
Yoshida still has the flu, so he won't be coming to school today.

body.p: Sometimes men may use じゃ is used instead of や. For example: こいつ、ワシのまごじゃ。
In formal settings, expressions other than や and じゃ are used. These more formal expression very by speaker and region in Kansai, but grossly:

いいですね。

body.p: The だ in the standard Japanese だから and だけど may become や.
The standard Japanese negative form じゃない may become やない in Kansai-ben. For more information, please see the Nやない page.

The standard progressive, conditional, or stative Vている may become Vてる or Vとる in Kansai-ben. Vてる obviously derives from Vている, while Vとる derives from Vておる. While originally the latter may have been considered more polite, it is now more about personal taste.
It should be noted that in casual speech, even standard Japanese may drop the い form いる in the Vている form.

A: 何してるん？
B: めがね、探してんねん*。

A: What are you doing?
B: I'm looking for my glasses.

body.p: * When Vてる and Vとる are used with sentence endings, the final る may become ん.

table.caption: Vとる
rows: あの人、ずっとこっちを見ているよ。気持ち悪いねえ。
あの人、ずっとこっち見とるで。気持ち悪いなあ。
That person has been staring at us the whole time. It's unnerving.

body.p: Vとう is more common than Vてる and Vとる in Kobe and its surrounding area.

body.h: Vてる and Vとる as conditional and stative forms

rows: この部屋、クーラーついている？
この部屋、クーラーついてる？
Is the air conditioner on in here?

body.h: ている form of いる = いてる

body.p: While there is no Vている form of いる in standard Japanese, there is in Kansai-ben--いてる and いとる. There is no such parallel for ある.

table.caption: いてる
rows: 今日はずっと家にいるよ。
今日はずっと家にいてるよ。
I'll be staying home all day today.

body.p: Vてある in standard Japanese, when used in the sense of preparation or state, may become Vたある in Kansai-ben

rows: ここに書いてあるじゃない。ちゃんと見てよ。
ここに書いたあるやん。ちゃんと見ぃや。
Look, it's written here. Take another look.

body.p: Vたある in Kansai-ben can also be used like Vている in standard Japanese when describing the state of something.

rows: あ、このパソコンこわれているよ。
あ、このパソコンこわれたあるで。

body.p: The standard Vておく, when used in a sentence to indicate preparation, may become Vとく in Kansai-ben. Similarly, Vないでおく may become Vんとく.
It should be noted that Vんとく may be also used as a suggestion and warning, in addition its usual "preparation" meaning.

rows: V (te-form but use と instead of final て) +く

table.caption: Vとく
rows: 今日、エリのたんじょうびだからケーキ買っておくよ。
今日、エリのたんじょうびやよってケーキ買うとくわ。
Today is Eri's birthday, so I'll buy a cake.

table.caption: Vんとく
rows: 今日は疲れているから飲みに行かないでおくよ。
今日はしんどいから飲みに行かんとくわ。
I'm tired so I'll pass on going out for drinks today.

body.h: Vとけへん, Vといて／Vとって

body.p: The Vておかない in standard Japanese may become Vとけへん in Kansai-ben. Similarly for Vておいて becoming Vといて or Vとって in Kansai-ben.

table.caption: Vとけへん
rows: 週末、パーティーするから、飲み物買っておかない？
週末、パーティーするから、飲み物買うとけへん？
There's a party this weekend, so should we buy some drinks?

table.caption: Vといて／Vとって
rows: まだ準備できていないんだ。先に行っておいて。

まだ準備できてないねん。先に行っといて。
まだ準備できてないねん。先に行っといて。
I'm not ready yet. You can go ahead.

body.p: Kansai-ben's Vんといて can be used like standard Japanese's Vないで(ください).

table.caption: Vんといて
rows: 私の部屋に勝手に入らないで。
うちの部屋に勝手に入らんといて。

body.h: Giving advice: Vとき, Vんとき

body.p: Vとき and Vんとき are used when giving advice and suggestions.

table.caption: Vとき
rows: 今日、帰り遅くなるから、先に寝てね。
今日、帰り遅なるよって、先に寝とき。
I'm going to come home late today, so don't wait up.

table.caption: Vんとき
rows: もう飲まないほうがいいよ。明日、二日酔いになるよ。
もう飲まんとき。明日、二日酔いになるで。
If you don't stop drinking, you'll have a hangover tomorrow.

body.p: Unlike standard Japanese, there are two types of potential form depending on the situation: ability potential and situational potential. The ability potential, ようV, is often used with question and negative (the negative form is ようVへん and ようV). The situational potential is the same as in standard Japanese.

rows: うちの弟、よう泳がへんねん。

table.caption: ようVん
rows: 足痛いから、走れないよ。
足痛いよって、よう走らんわ。
I can't run because my legs hurt.

table.caption: ようVん
rows: それはひみつだから、言えないんだ。
それはひみつやから、言えへんねん。
I can't tell you because it's a secret.

body.h: The difference between ようVへん and ようVん

body.p: While ようVへん is used when the subject is third person (he/she/it), ようVん is mainly used when the subject is first person (I). It should be noted that ようVん can be used with questions when the subject is the second person (you).

body.h: Subjectivity with ようV and ようVん

body.p: ようVん is used not only with the ability negative potential but also when expressing disgust, blame, and surprise. In the latter case, the よう in ようVん is the same meaning of よく in standard Japanese.

table.caption: disgust/blame
rows: そんな恥ずかしいことよくできるね。
そんな恥ずかしいことようするなあ。
I can't do that--it would be so embarrassing.

table.caption: surprise
rows: あんた、よう食べるなあ。
You sure do eat a lot.

table.caption: disgust/blame
rows: そんなひどいことできないよ。
そんなえげつないことようせんわ。
I couldn't do something that awful.

body.p: The common phrase "よう言わんわ" does not just mean to "not have much to say", but implies that the speaker is strongly disgusted and they have nothing to say about the topic.

rows: あいつ、またうわきしたのか。もう、何も言う言葉がないよ。
あいつ、またうわき*しよったんか。もう、よう言わんわ。
Has he been cheating again? I don't have anything more to say (about that).

body.p: *うわき = unfaithful; cheat on someone

body.h: When to use V (potential) へん and V (potential) ん

body.p: Only V (potential) へん and V (potential) ん can be used when the speaker wants to do something but they are unable to. ようVへん and ようVん cannot be used in that case.

table.caption: V (potential) へん
rows: 今、ダイエット中だから、甘いもの食べられないんだ。
今、ダイエット中やから、甘いもん食べられへんねん。
Since I'm on a diet, I can't have anything sweet.

body.p: There are some differences between the causative forms of standard Japanese and Kansai-ben. For su-verbs and suru-verbs, whereas the negative causative form is always long form in standard Japanese, the short form can be used in Kansai-ben. This is also true for the short causative passive form in Kansai-ben (while it should not be used in the standard). In general, the causative long form is rarely used in Kansai-ben.

body.p: In business, instead of directly saying "no", 考えときます is often used to indicate that negotiations are over (loosely) or to indicate that the speaker is not interested. However, the causative 考えさせてもらいます is different; in this case, there is a chance that speaker is actually going to respond positively.

body.p: In Kansai-ben, the final う sound of the volitional form is often omitted (Dropping "う"), so the volitional form may become V(よ).

rows: 明日、学校休もうと思っているんだ。
明日、学校休も思てるねん。
I'm thinking about not going to school tomorrow.

body.p: There are some cases where the te-form of i-adjectives in Kansai-ben is different from those in standard Japanese. Please pay attention to the sound before the final い--when it is [a], [i], [u], or [o] it may change.

body.h: When the sound before the final い is [a]

body.p: Replace the [a] with [o] and add うて to the end.

body.h: When the sound before the final い is [i]

body.p: There are two cases: -しい becomes -しゅう and -きい becomes -きゅう before adding the て.

たのしいて

body.h: When the sound before the final い is [u] or [o]

body.p: Replace the final い with an う and add て. It should be noted that the う is often omitted (dropping "う").

Vやる and Vよる are used to express a speaker's strong feelings, such as surprise or contempt, when the subject is neither the speaker nor the listener (a third-person subject). There is no such a grammar point in standard Japanese.

rows:
行きやる
行きよる

table.caption: Surprise
rows: あいつ、とうとう結婚したよ。
あいつ、とうとう結婚しよったで。

table.caption: Contempt
rows: あいつ、またふられたらしいよ。
あいつ、またふられよったらしいで。

table.caption: Suspicion
rows: あいつ、ここで何していたんだ。
あいつ、ここで何してやったんや。
I wonder what he was doing here.

body.p: In general, Vやる is used by women and Vよる is used by men, but women could use Vよる if they want to show stronger emotion.

body.h: やる/よる vs. はる

body.p: You may notice that the usage of Vやる and Vよる is similar to Vはる. However, it should be noted that Vはる is usually used when referring to strangers, people of higher status, or people you respect, while Vやる and Vよる are used for family members, close friends, or inferiors.

body.h: The feelings that Vやる and Vよる can express

body.p: While Vやる and Vよる can express speaker's feelings such as surprise and contempt, there are cases where they do not imply any strong feelings.

rows: 昨日、あなたのおばあさん、公園で寝ていたよ。
昨日、あんたのおばあちゃん、公園で寝てやったで。
Yesterday, your grandma was sleeping in the park.

body.p: V (negative stem) +はる
In Osaka, the affirmative stem form is used instead of the negative stem form.
The honorifics expression of the irregular verbs 来る and する are きはる and しはる respectively. There is also a Vやはる form that can be used with the preceding verbs as well as いる.
When はる is used with the ている form, Vたはる is used instead of Vてはる.
It should be noted that since おる is used instead of いる in the area of Kobe, there is no Vている, but instead Vておる is used. In addition, in this case, です is used instead of ます.
Vはる is used not only as an honorific expression, but also can be used to increase politeness or when trying to describe something objectively.

あの子、どうして泣いているんだろう。
I wonder why the kid is crying.

title: Vowels

body.p: There are five vowels in Kansai-ben: あ, い, う, え, and お--the same as standard Japanese. According to Yamashita (2004) , Kansai-ben is an easy to understand dialect for Japanese learners because people tend to pronounce vowels more clearly.

To take a single case, unlike standard Japanese where [i] and [u] sound are often devoiced, devoicing these vowels rarely occurs in Kansai-ben. For example, in standard Japanese 聞く is usually pronounced [k(i)ku], 行きますか [(i)kimasuka], and です [des(u)]. However, in Kansai-ben, people clearly pronounce these [i] and [u] sounds.
Another case is the pronunciation of う. In Kansai, people round their lips more than they do in standard Japanese. This has the effect of making the sound more clear.
Besides the above two examples, there are three broad characteristics of Kansai-ben vowels: palatalization, vowel extension, and the dropping of "う".

refs: Yamashita, Y. (2004) Kansai-ben Koogi, Tokyo: Kodansha

body.p: In Kansai-ben, some speakers (usually older) may replace the ひ sound in a word with a し sound. For example, standard “shichi” may become “hichi” in Kansai-ben.
For some older people in certain parts, such as Wakayama, the “z” sound used in some words may become “d.” For example, the standard “zenzen” would become “denden.”

body.p: Palatalization is when the flat of the tongue gets close to the roof of the mouth (palate). Since the い sound is pronounced more clearly in Kansai-ben than it is in standard Japanese, it affects the consonant right before い (causing palatalization). Below are some examples of palatalization in Kansai-ben, with their standard counterparts for comparison.

In Kansai-ben, there is more accent than there are in standard Japanese--accent is very important in Kansai-ben. While listening to the Kansai accent can be useful in understanding and producing it, it is important to understand the underlying characteristics that compose it. All words can be placed into one of four groups defined by two characteristics.
The first characteristic is the pitch of the first mora. All words are classified into two groups: group H where the first mora's pitch is high and group L where it's low.

The second characteristic is called the downstep. A downstep is where a high pitched mora's sound starts to fall. A downstep can occur anywhere or not at all, but if the mora starts with a low pitch it cannot (naturally) occur there. Also, it's rare for the downstep to occur in the final aremora of a longer word. In special mora--nasals (ん), long vowels (もう, etc.), and long consonants (the っ in 切った)--downsteps can occur in Kansai-ben, but don't appear in standard Japanese. See "downstep examples" for the examples.

After a downstep occurs in a word, no more high pitched mora will occur, the same as in standard Japanese. It's good to note that one can discriminate between compound words versus separate words using this (e.g., cheese cake, cheesecake).
To practice listening for these characteristics, please see the intonation differences between standard Japanese and Kansai-ben in common phrases and sentences.
